{{DISPLAYTITLE:The three axioms}}
{{Plebeian|Lean theorem prover/Explainers/What the axioms are}}
{{Lean theorem prover map}}

Lean's type theory, with its dependent functions, universes, inductive types and quotients,
is extended in the core library by three '''axioms''': propositional extensionality
(<code>propext</code>), the soundness of quotients (<code>Quot.sound</code>) and global
choice (<code>Classical.choice</code>). An axiom is a constant with a type and no
definition; it does not reduce, and the compiler cannot generate code for it.<ref name="refman-axioms">''The Lean Language Reference'', version 4.34.0, chapter 8 "Axioms": the introduction, §8.2 "Consistency", §8.3 "Reduction", §8.4 "Standard Axioms" and §8.5 "Displaying Axiom Dependencies". https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Axioms/</ref> Lean records, for every
definition and theorem, which axioms it depends on, and prints the list on request. This
page states the three as Lean prints them, says what each makes possible, shows the
dependency audit on examples, and sets out the further axioms that are not mathematics at
all.

== As Lean prints them ==

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
#print propext
#print Quot.sound
#print Classical.choice
</pre>
<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
axiom propext : ∀ {a b : Prop}, (a ↔ b) → a = b
axiom Quot.sound.{u} : ∀ {α : Sort u} {r : α → α → Prop} {a b : α}, r a b → Quot.mk r a = Quot.mk r b
axiom Classical.choice.{u} : {α : Sort u} → Nonempty α → α
</pre>

In Lean 4.34.1 <code>propext</code> is stated in the file <code>Init/Core.lean</code>, and
the other two in <code>Init/Prelude.lean</code>.<ref name="src">Lean 4 source, version 4.34.1: files <code>src/Init/Core.lean</code> (<code>propext</code>), <code>src/Init/Prelude.lean</code> (<code>Quot.sound</code>, <code>Classical.choice</code>, <code>sorryAx</code>) and <code>src/Init/Classical.lean</code> (the proof of <code>Classical.em</code>). Apache License 2.0. https://github.com/leanprover/lean4/tree/v4.34.1/src/Init</ref> As rules, with
<math>a, b : \mathrm{Prop}</math>:

:<math>\frac{\Gamma \vdash h : a \leftrightarrow b}{\Gamma \vdash \mathrm{propext}\,h : a = b} \qquad \frac{\Gamma \vdash p : r\,a\,b}{\Gamma \vdash \mathrm{Quot.sound}\,p : \mathrm{Quot.mk}\,r\,a = \mathrm{Quot.mk}\,r\,b} \qquad \frac{\Gamma \vdash h : \mathrm{Nonempty}\,\alpha}{\Gamma \vdash \mathrm{Classical.choice}\,h : \alpha}</math>

The first two conclude equations, which are propositions. The third concludes an element of
an arbitrary type. That difference decides how each one interacts with computation.

== What each makes possible ==

'''Propositional extensionality''' says that logically equivalent propositions are equal,
so that one may be replaced by the other in any context. The reference manual notes that
the ordinary connectives respect logical equivalence provably, without the axiom, but that
it is needed for an unknown predicate <code>P : Prop → Prop</code> applied to equivalent
arguments, and for equality between propositions itself.<ref name="refman-props">''The Lean Language Reference'', version 4.34.0, §4.2 "Propositions" (the axiom <code>propext</code> and its documentation). https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/The-Type-System/Propositions/</ref> It is
valid intuitionistically.<ref name="refman-props" /> ''Theorem Proving in Lean 4'' adds that
it agrees with set-theoretic readings in which every proposition is either empty or a
one-element set.<ref name="tpil">Jeremy Avigad, Leonardo de Moura, Soonho Kong and Sebastian Ullrich, ''Theorem Proving in Lean 4'', chapter 12 "Axioms and Computation". https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/Axioms-and-Computation/</ref>

'''Quotient soundness''' identifies the classes of related elements in a
[[Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Quotient types|quotient type]]. It is also the only
axiom behind function extensionality, which Lean proves as a theorem from quotients; the
proof is on [[Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Propositional equality|propositional equality]]. With <code>propext</code> it gives an extensional theory of sets represented as
predicates: two predicates true of the same elements are equal.<ref name="tpil" />

'''Global choice''' turns a proof that a type is inhabited into an element of it.
<code>Nonempty α</code> is a proposition, and a proof of it carries no information about
which element exists. <code>Classical.choice</code> nevertheless returns one, and returns the
same one for any proof, since all proofs of a proposition are equal. ''Theorem Proving in
Lean 4'' derives from it the principle of indefinite description, and, with the other two
axioms, excluded middle, the decidability of every proposition and Hilbert's epsilon
operator.<ref name="tpil" /> That derivation is
[[Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Classical logic from choice|classical logic from choice]].

The first two can block evaluation in Lean's kernel, because a cast along an equation proved by
an axiom does not reduce, but they are compatible with compiled code, which erases proofs.
Choice is not: it manufactures data from a proposition, and definitions that use it for data
must be marked <code>noncomputable</code>.<ref name="tpil" />

== The audit: #print axioms ==

<code>#print axioms</code> lists every axiom a constant depends on, directly or through the
definitions and theorems it uses.<ref name="refman-axioms" /> Five small theorems show
the range from none to all three:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
theorem two_add_two : 2 + 2 = 4 := rfl

theorem and_swap (p q : Prop) : p ∧ q ↔ q ∧ p :=
  ⟨fun ⟨hp, hq⟩ => ⟨hq, hp⟩, fun ⟨hq, hp⟩ => ⟨hp, hq⟩⟩

theorem and_swap_eq (p q : Prop) : (p ∧ q) = (q ∧ p) :=
  propext (and_swap p q)

theorem add_zero_fun : (fun n : Nat => n + 0) = (fun n => n) :=
  funext fun _ => rfl

theorem em' (p : Prop) : p ∨ ¬p := Classical.em p

#print axioms two_add_two
#print axioms and_swap
#print axioms and_swap_eq
#print axioms add_zero_fun
#print axioms em'
</pre>
<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
'two_add_two' does not depend on any axioms
'and_swap' does not depend on any axioms
'and_swap_eq' depends on axioms: [propext]
'add_zero_fun' depends on axioms: [Quot.sound]
'em'' depends on axioms: [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]
</pre>

Here the computation checked by <code>rfl</code> and the logical equivalence need nothing, the
equation between propositions needs <code>propext</code>, and the equation between functions
needs <code>Quot.sound</code>, through <code>funext</code>. Excluded middle needs all three,
because the proof of <code>Classical.em</code> in the core library uses choice,
<code>propext</code> and <code>funext</code>.<ref name="src" />

== sorry and sorryAx ==

The term <code>sorry</code> closes any goal. It elaborates to the axiom
<code>sorryAx</code>, which inhabits every type, and so it is used for unfinished work and
never belongs in a finished proof.<ref name="refman-axioms" />

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
#print sorryAx

theorem unfinished : 1 = 2 := sorry

theorem uses_unfinished : 2 = 3 := congrArg (· + 1) unfinished

#print axioms uses_unfinished
</pre>
<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
axiom sorryAx.{u} : (α : Sort u) → Bool → α
'uses_unfinished' depends on axioms: [sorryAx]
</pre>

Lean warns once, with <code>declaration uses `sorry`</code>, at <code>unfinished</code>,
where <code>sorry</code> is written. The
theorem <code>uses_unfinished</code> raises no warning of its own, yet it proves a falsehood,
and only the axiom list shows why. The reference manual makes the same point about the
editor's check marks: they appear even when a dependency uses <code>sorry</code>, and
printing the axioms is what detects it.<ref name="refman-validating">''The Lean Language Reference'', version 4.34.0, "Validating a Lean Proof", sections "The Blue Double Check Marks", "Printing Axioms" and "On Lean.trustCompiler (up to Lean 4.28.0)". https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/ValidatingProofs/</ref>

== Axioms that are not mathematics ==

Any user can write an axiom, and Lean accepts it. Lean cannot check that a
new axiom is consistent with the others.<ref name="refman-axioms" />

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
axiom everything_is_equal : ∀ (a b : Nat), a = b

theorem one_eq_two : 1 = 2 := everything_is_equal 1 2

#print axioms one_eq_two
</pre>

The last line prints <code>'one_eq_two' depends on axioms: [everything_is_equal]</code>.
The theorem is checked and accepted; the audit is what exposes its premise.

An axiom can also be harmless on its own and inconsistent with the standard three. The
reference manual's example is a "free theorem" of parametricity, which says that a function
polymorphic in the element type of a list commutes with mapping over the list. With excluded
middle every proposition is decidable, so a function can test whether its type argument is
<code>Nat</code> and behave differently when it is. That function is not parametric, and
together with the free theorem it proves <code>False</code>.<ref name="refman-axioms" />

The core library itself states three further axioms, <code>Lean.trustCompiler</code>,
<code>Lean.ofReduceBool</code> and <code>Lean.ofReduceNat</code>. The reference manual
describes them as mathematically trivial: they mark proofs that depend on the correctness of
the whole compiler rather than only on Lean's small kernel.<ref name="refman-axioms" /> The
tactic <code>native_decide</code>, which settles a decidable statement by running compiled
code, creates a dedicated axiom for each use, stating exactly the fact the compiled code
asserted:<ref name="refman-axioms" />

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
theorem big : 123456 * 654321 = 80779853376 := by native_decide

#print axioms big
</pre>

Lean 4.34.1 prints <code>'big' depends on axioms: [big._native.native_decide.ax_1_1]</code>.
Such a theorem rests on the correctness of the whole compiler, not only on Lean's kernel and
the three axioms: each use of the tactic widens what has to be trusted.<ref name="refman-validating" />

== Why audit per theorem ==

The three standard axioms are, in the reference manual's words, "known to be
consistent".<ref name="refman-axioms" /> Carneiro's model of Lean's type theory in set
theory, published in 2019, covers all three axioms together;<ref name="carneiro">Mario Carneiro, ''The Type Theory of Lean'', Master's thesis, Carnegie Mellon University, 2019; abstract, §2.7 (pp. 12–13) and Corollary 6.8 (p. 41). https://github.com/digama0/lean-type-theory/releases/tag/v1.0</ref> it is described, with its limits, in
[[Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Consistency and the metatheory|consistency and the metatheory]].
Every other axiom is a premise the reader has to accept separately. The manual's guide to
validating a proof therefore asks that <code>#print axioms</code> report only
<code>propext</code>, <code>Classical.choice</code> and <code>Quot.sound</code>: a
<code>sorryAx</code> means an incomplete proof, <code>Lean.trustCompiler</code> means trust in
native evaluation, and anything else means a custom axiom on which the result is
conditional.<ref name="refman-validating" />

A list of axioms also says what kind of result a theorem is. A theorem whose list omits
<code>Classical.choice</code> uses no classical reasoning obtained from it, and one with an
empty list holds in the type theory alone. The check can be made permanent. The manual suggests pairing <code>#print axioms</code> with
<code>#guard_msgs</code>, so that a change in a library one depends on cannot silently add
an axiom:<ref name="refman-axioms" />

<pre class="lean lean-cont" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
/-- info: 'two_add_two' does not depend on any axioms -/
#guard_msgs in
#print axioms two_add_two
</pre>

If the proof of <code>two_add_two</code> ever came to depend on an axiom, the message would
change, and this command would fail.
